items.question: What draws you toward reasoning and reinforcement learning after your earlier work on architectures and pre-training?
items.object: Reasoning and reinforcement learning as a research direction
items.answer: I think I miss research a lot, doing research. Not super fundamental research, but close to model research, right? I really miss being at the frontier and trying to go beyond that. So I really miss that a lot. There was some inclination that reasoning is the next frontier, and that's obviously the most rewarding research path, especially this year. I spent a lot of my past life, I call it the past arc, working on architectures and pre-training. But now I'm more conditioned into RL research. To be honest I had almost no RL background coming back. But RL is the main means of modeling these days, and I think it was pretty easy to jump back in.

items.question: How do you understand the distinction between on-policy and off-policy learning in LLM training?
items.object: On-policy versus off-policy learning in LLM training
items.answer: I think the biggest analogy of on-policy and off-policy is basically: off-policy is when you SFT something. You take some other model, a larger model's stuff, and then it's off-policy. Somebody else's generated outputs, trajectories, and whatever. On-policy is mainly the core idea of modern LLM RL, where you generate and then reward the model based on its own generations, and then the model trains on its own generations. So it's a bit like self-distillation to some extent: the model generates its own output, and then you reward it and it trains on its own output. On-polici-ness is basically this idea of the model training on its own outputs and letting the model generate its own trajectories, and then letting some reward verify it, and then the model trains on its own outputs. I think this is more generalizable in general. I think there's still a lot of stuff to be done about the gap between SFT and RL itself.

items.question: How do you think people should adjust their beliefs when they encounter an example that breaks their existing worldview?
items.object: Human learning rates and updating beliefs after being wrong
items.answer: I do tell people to keep an idea of their own learning rate and to be wary of it being too low. For example, if you've been wrong once, you should ask, where else have I been wrong? Typically, people update slower than they should when they have been wrong. What is it, stubbornness? I don't know, is that the right word for it? It could be that they are too Bayesian when actually their prior assumptions were wrong and they need to completely throw out their previous assumptions, because one counterexample invalidates all prior experience. Your entire world model is wrong. Throw it away. Let's say you live for 10 years under some assumptions and you have one example that breaks your narrative. You shouldn't be like, okay, now I have a 2% update. No. Actually, you should be like, oh, something's really freaking changed. Everything I've ever seen for the last 10 years is probably wrong. What else am I wrong in? Update 20%, update 50%, not 2%. You know what I mean?

items.question: How do you think about adjusting your intellectual learning rate when a new AI paradigm challenges your world model?
items.object: Adjusting one's intellectual learning rate when new AI paradigms invalidate existing beliefs
items.answer: My direct example is the whole getting into AI stuff. I was watching GANs for 10 years. Has it been 10 years? 2012? 2013? Time flies, yeah. I was watching GANs and I was like, okay, this is cool. It's getting more detail, not that impressive. Then all of a sudden Stable Diffusion came out and you can run it on your laptop. And that was my learning rate. Okay, my mental model of generative images did not include this. I was like, okay, I am very wrong and I need to pivot everything. And that's how I started Latent Space. So, what does it mean that your learning rate is high? Yes, I will nudge it up. I schedule my learning rate, because a world model has been violated. Okay, I think it's a good strategy. I think this also brings a little bit to light when new paradigms happen, how fast people are to adopt it or invalidate their understanding of things. As scientists, a lot of times we do have to, as people progress, keep invalidating our own world model.

items.question: How do you think about the limits of encoding tool capabilities, such as a calculator or a Lean system, in a model’s parameters?
items.object: Encoding tool capabilities in a model’s parameters
items.answer: I mean, it's just whether at the end of the day you believe in this connection: it's one model, lots of parameters. I mean there's also tool use. But to some extent, I think we should be able to get to a point where, in the past when LLMs first started, the model couldn't even be a calculator. Now it can somewhat be a calculator. So technically a tool like a calculator is somewhat encoded in the parameters of the model. I think we eventually get to a point where whether there are things that cannot be expressed in the parameters of the model is an open question. We don't know where the limit is, but I think we will keep pushing this limit. Whether something like a Lean system or some other things to solve other things, like maybe a physics engine, is still—we continue to push that boundary.

items.question: How did you approach working together as captains while training the model for the International Mathematical Olympiad?
items.object: Coordination among the four captains training the IMO model
items.answer: I think there were four captains for the IMO. Two from London, Jonathan was from Mountain View, I was from Singapore. So four of us basically trained this model together. One interesting thing was that we were all in different time zones. There's something interesting about passing on the job. There's no fixed rule for how to work together between captains. It's more like, "Oh, I'm going to board the plane now. I'll be AFK for 12 hours," so someone takes it, just babysitting around. Sometimes there are bugs and stuff, the job comes down sometimes. It's very ad hoc, very much between the captains how we decide to work together. I think it was an interesting time because we were all flying. The London folks didn't have to fly, but I had to fly and Jonathan had to fly. When you visit another country, another office, you have many meetings. I was in and out of meetings, and it was pretty interesting. Nobody really knew whether we would get a gold at that time because the IMO actually hadn't happened.

items.question: What does Gemini’s IMO gold achievement tell you about the pace of AI progress?
items.object: AI progress as reflected in Gemini’s IMO gold achievement
items.answer: Then the silver helped, right, from last year. items.question: How do you understand reasoning in today's language models?
items.object: Reasoning in language models
items.answer: I think these days reasoning itself is very vague and open. Different people will have different definitions of what reasoning is. I agree that chain of thought is basically what people associate with reasoning, and obviously it's what happens in the thinking. These days, like I said earlier, reasoning and RL are almost the same. It's anything that's post-training to elicit capabilities. The actual technical definition of reasoning is making models better with thinking and post-training. Basically RL-ing the model to think better. Thinking is more like thinking traces and thought trajectories. There's also this line of work for latent thinking and stuff like that, whether latent thinking and discrete token thinking are going to be the same thing or something like that. It's an open question.

items.question: How do you think about latent thinking as an alternative to having language models reason through discrete tokens?
items.object: Latent thinking in language models
items.answer: I don't remember what's the name, these academic papers that do this, latent tokens or like they basically, instead of decoding the discrete tokens, you simulate this by doing this in latent space. When you do chain-of-thought thinking and reasoning, you decode extra tokens hiding in the thinking tag. But latent thinking is basically you just don't decode tokens. You don't bother. It might start speaking the native language of thinking, which is numbers, not passing it through some filter of English. Sometimes it might start thinking Chinese or something else. Generally, I don't really believe that model thoughts have to be the same as human thoughts. In ML, I'm more of the school of thought of let the model do whatever it wants.

items.question: How do you think geography matters in AI research when your collaborators are spread internationally?
items.object: Geography and national identity in AI research
items.answer: I don't even really know what countries mean anymore when it comes to research or AI in general, because this thing is inherently international from the start. It's also related to identity, because you move from SF and Singapore quite a bit, right? I was in Mountain View one or two weeks ago, and I'm here, but almost all of my stuff, aside from my family, is people I talk to somehow in the Bay Area, because of work and everything. Geography matters. Firstly, the most logistical thing is probably the time zone. So you literally want 24-hour coverage around the world.

items.question: How do you understand your team's ability to attract AI talent from the region to Singapore?

items.question: How do you think about growing your team for RL reasoning work on Gemini and Gemini Deep Think?

items.question: How do you think about the pressure on graduate students to demonstrate research taste?
items.object: Demonstrating research taste as a graduate student
items.answer: I care about this in some ways. The research directions and work that I do are a little bit of that. It's low accountability for me because obviously it's just thought experiments. But for a lot of people their career is bounded by whether they can demonstrate research taste in the short three or four years that they have. It's more about how you're going to prove yourself.
